ety.text: From Middle English jumpen (“to walk quickly, run, jump”), probably of Middle Low German or North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gumpōną ~ *gumbōną (“to hop, skip, bounce”), an iterative verb. The OED suggests an imitative origin. Related to jumble. In the sense “to propel oneself” it displaced leap partially and spring largely.
Compare French jupe (“a long petticoat, a skirt”) and English jupon.

senses.d: To propel oneself rapidly upward, downward and/or in any horizontal direction such that momentum causes the body to become airborne.
ex: The boy jumped over a fence.
Kangaroos are known for their ability to jump high.

senses.d: To cause oneself to leave an elevated location and fall downward.
ex: She is going to jump from the diving board.

senses.d: To pass by means of a spring or leap; to overleap.
ex: to jump a stream

senses.d: To employ a parachute to leave an aircraft or elevated location.
To jerk the body involuntarily in response to a sudden or unexpected stimulus.
ex: That balloon popping made me jump.
He jumped when he looked up to see a man standing before him.

senses.d: To drop sharply downward at the sound of a bowstring release or the fire of a gun.
ex: The deer jumped the string, so the archer missed his target.
The buck jumped at the shot of the rifle.

senses.d: To increase sharply, to rise, to shoot up.
ex: Share prices jumped by 10% after the company announced record profits.

senses.d: To employ a move in certain board games where one game piece is moved from one legal position to another passing over the position of another piece.
ex: The player's knight jumped the opponent's bishop.

senses.d: To move to a position (in a queue/line) that is further forward.
ex: I hate it when people jump the queue.

senses.d: To pass (a traffic light) when it is indicating that one should stop.
The act of jumping; a leap; a spring; a bound.
ex: To advance by jumps.

senses.d: An effort; an attempt; a venture.
ex: Our fortune lies / Upon this jump.

senses.d: A dislocation in a stratum; a fault.
An abrupt interruption of level in a piece of brickwork or masonry.
An instance of propelling oneself upwards.
ex: The boy took a skip and a jump down the lane.

senses.d: An object which causes one to jump; a ramp.
ex: The skier flew off the jump and landed perfectly.

senses.d: An instance of causing oneself to fall from an elevated location.
ex: There were a couple of jumps from the bridge.

senses.d: An instance of employing a parachute to leave an aircraft or elevated location.
ex: She was terrified before the jump, but was thrilled to be skydiving.

senses.d: An instance of reacting to a sudden stimulus by jerking the body.
A jumping move in a board game.
ex: the knight's jump in chess

senses.d: Exactly; precisely
ex:
Thus twice before, and jump at this dead hour,
With martial stalk hath he gone by our watch.

senses.d: Exact; matched; fitting; precise.
ex: jump names

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English jumper From jump + -er.

From the term jump (“short coat”) + -er, originally in sailors' jargon, ultimately of uncertain origin. Jump is possibly from Scottish English jupe (“man's loose jacket or tunic”), from Middle English juype, gype, joupe, from Old French jupe, juppe, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba); see also jibba. Cognate with Middle Low German jōpe, gōpe (“waistcoat, jacket”), German Joppe (“jacket”). Alternatively, perhaps derived from jump.
